cards.front: What does a single letter (like $n$) represent in an algebraic proof?
cards.back: A general number (representing every possible case).

options.text: A general number (representing every possible case).
options.explanation: The letter $n$ is treated as arbitrary, so reasoning that works for $n$ applies to every number covered by the proof rather than one selected example.

options.text: A fixed unknown number (representing only one hidden value).
options.explanation: Treating $n$ as one fixed unknown confuses algebraic proof with solving an equation. The letter represents a general number so the argument covers every possible case.

options.text: A chosen example number (representing one possible case).
options.explanation: Checking one chosen example can illustrate a claim but cannot prove it generally. In an algebraic proof, $n$ represents a general number covering every possible case.

options.text: A positive whole number (representing only counting-number cases).
options.explanation: A letter is not automatically restricted to positive whole numbers unless the proof states that restriction. Here, $n$ represents a general number and every possible case.
